entities.summary:
The Royal Geographical Society (RGS), established in 1830, is a prominent British learned society dedicated to the advancement of geography and exploration. Headquartered in Lowther Lodge, London, it has played a pivotal role in the development of geographical knowledge and exploration methodologies, influencing the way geography is taught and understood globally. Notable figures associated with the Society include explorers such as David Livingstone and Sir Ernest Shackleton, who contributed significantly to the Society's mission of promoting geographical research and understanding. The Society's impact extends beyond national borders, as its efforts have influenced global exploration and scientific inquiry into the natural world.

Throughout its history, the RGS has facilitated numerous significant expeditions, including the mapping of Africa and the polar regions. The Society was instrumental in the establishment of the first comprehensive maps of various regions, helping to chart territories previously unknown to Europeans. In 1884, the Society organized the International Meridian Conference, which established the Greenwich Meridian as the prime meridian, fundamentally shaping global navigation and timekeeping standards. With its support for exploration and research, the RGS has published thousands of works, creating a vast repository of knowledge that continues to be utilized by scholars and explorers alike.
